title: The Telephone
objective: After this level you can explain how early telephones turned voices into electric signals.
summary: A telephone turns sound into a current shaped like the sound wave, then back into sound. Bell got the 1876 patent; Gray filed the same day and Meucci earlier.

cards.headline: On one day in 1876, two inventors filed papers on the same idea.
cards.body: On February 14, 1876, Alexander Graham Bell applied for a patent on sending sound by wire. Britannica says Elisha Gray filed a caveat, a formal notice of an invention in progress, on a similar method hours later that same day, though even the order is disputed. Bell's patent came through on March 7. The argument never quite ended.

cards.headline: A current shaped like your voice
cards.body: Level 42's telegraph only switched current on and off. A telephone does something subtler. Your voice makes a thin diaphragm vibrate, and the transmitter turns those vibrations into a current that rises and falls like the sound wave itself. At the other end, the changing current drives an electromagnet that shakes a second diaphragm, rebuilding the sound. The wire carries a copy of your voice, drawn in electricity.

cards.fact: March 10, 1876: "Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you."
cards.context: That's how Bell's lab notes record the first intelligible speech his apparatus carried. His idea leaned on Level 8's induction: a sound wave vibrating one membrane would induce a voltage in a coil, and that current could make a second, connected membrane vibrate the same way. History's first phone call was, fittingly, a request for company.

cards.headline: Who invented the telephone? It depends who you ask.
cards.body: Gray's caveat described a liquid transmitter, and Bell's March 10 success used a liquid transmitter too, one reason the fight lasted. Earlier still, Antonio Meucci had filed a caveat of his own but couldn't pay the $10 fee to keep it after 1874. In 2002 the US House of Representatives passed a resolution honoring his work on the telephone. Bell holds the patent; the credit is still argued.

cards.headline: Telephone: connected
learned: Sound becomes a current shaped like the sound wave
An electromagnet and diaphragm turn it back into sound
Bell's patent came in 1876; Gray filed the same day
Meucci's earlier caveat keeps the credit debate alive

questions.prompt: How does a telephone's transmitter send your voice down the wire?

options.label: As light flashing inside the cable
options.rationale: No light involved: it's a changing current.

options.label: As dots and dashes tapped on a key
As the sound itself, piped along a tube
options.rationale: The sound becomes an electric current.

options.label: As a current that rises and falls like the sound wave

questions.explanation: The diaphragm's vibrations become a current with the same pattern as the sound wave; the receiver turns it back into sound.

questions.prompt: Why is the question "who invented the telephone?" still argued today?

options.label: Several inventors filed on similar ideas around the same time
No one was ever granted a telephone patent
options.rationale: Bell was granted one on March 7, 1876.

options.label: Bell's first call failed to carry any speech
options.rationale: It carried intelligible speech on March 10, 1876.

options.label: The first telephone was built in 2002
options.rationale: 2002 is when the House honored Meucci.

questions.explanation: Gray filed a caveat the same day as Bell's application, and Meucci had filed one earlier, so Bell's patent never settled the credit.

questions.prompt: Bell reasoned that a vibrating membrane could induce a voltage in a coil. Which Level 8 discovery was he relying on?

options.label: A changing magnetic field makes a current flow
Energy turns mostly into heat in a bulb

questions.explanation: Faraday's induction: a changing magnetic field in a coil makes a current. A vibrating membrane can supply the change.
